Quadratic fields and their ideals

Abstract

004 - Ideals and Dedekind domains and 005 - Fractional ideals and the ideal class group develop the theory of a Dedekind domain without ever exhibiting one. This chapter produces the ring the whole course is about, the ring of integers of a quadratic field, proves it is Dedekind, and then computes with its ideals: each has a canonical basis, a norm, and satisfies
Everything here is elementary arithmetic of lattices in , and all of it feeds 007 - The narrow class group and the form class group.

The set of all algebraic integers of is denoted ; by definition it is the integral closure of in .

Note

Every is an algebraic number, being a finite hence algebraic extension of : the powers are elements of an -dimensional -vector space, so they satisfy a linear relation. Constructing an integral basis

A -basis of is called an integral basis. The finiteness proof above gives a construction: start with an explicit order , use the trace pairing to place inside a computable larger lattice, and test the finitely many cosets modulo for integrality. The integral representatives, together with a basis of , generate ; Hermite normal form then extracts a basis.

    and set . The Hermite remainder construction shows that these represent , hence the represent .

    By the characteristic-polynomial criterion, this is equivalent to . Test all coefficients: norm and trace alone do not suffice in general. Integrality is constant on each coset modulo , since and algebraic integers form a ring. Thus, if is the finite set of retained representatives,

Apply column Hermite reduction to the integer generator matrix ; discard the zero columns and call the remaining matrix . All matrix operations are exact over or , and step 4 has only tests, proving termination. This is a general finite construction, although exhaustive enumeration can be expensive. It does not assume that itself has a power basis.

The rank comes from the product formula, which confines logarithms of units to the codimension-one hyperplane ; Minkowski's Convex Body Theorem is the input proving that the image fills up to bounded error rather than lying in a smaller subspace.

An order is a lattice that happens to be a ring

The two conditions pull in opposite directions and that is the whole point:

  • full is a size condition, spans , so is a rank- lattice of
  • ring with identity requires and , so has multiplication and the same identity as

Multiplicative closure alone is insufficient: is a full -module closed under multiplication, but is not an order because it does not contain . Similarly, a nonzero proper integral ideal of is full and closed under multiplication but is not an order. An ideal containing would equal .

Being finitely generated over and a ring makes every element of an order integral, which is why contains them all: The ring of integers is the maximal order. For the orders are classified by their discriminant, one for each , and they are the rings of Quadratic order.

Idea

This is Gaussian elimination using Euclidean division over . A nonzero remainder replaces the pivot by a smaller positive integer; one never divides a column by a nonunit.

Note
  • Allowed moves. Swap two columns, change a column's sign, or apply with and . Each is multiplication on the right by a unimodular matrix; its inverse is integral.
  • Why columns. The columns are generators, and . Every column operation acts on all its coordinates. A row operation gives , whose columns generate in the original coordinates. To interpret it as the same abstract lattice, change the ambient basis from the row of vectors to : .
  • No arbitrary division. Replacing the column by changes the generated subgroup. Only multiplication by the units is allowed as a scaling operation.

Proof and reduction algorithm

  • Work with the whole matrix throughout. For , use only columns ; these already have zeros in rows .
    1. Choose a pivot. Row among those columns contains a nonzero entry, since the remaining square block is nonsingular. Move one to by a column swap and make it positive, calling it .
    2. Perform Euclid across row . For , write the current entry , with , and apply . If , swap and restart with pivot ; otherwise that entry is now zero. Each restart strictly decreases the positive pivot, so eventually the row is in columns , with .
    3. Recurse on the upper left block. Freeze column and proceed to . Operations on columns preserve the zeros below them. The result is upper triangular with positive diagonal.
    4. Normalize the entries above the diagonal. After completing all stages, for and every , divide the current by and apply . This puts in . Column is zero below row , so rows already normalized remain unchanged. This explains why normalization runs from bottom to top.
      Every move is unimodular, so their product gives . This is the last-coordinate version of the triangular basis construction.

Warning
  • Hermite pivots have no general divisibility chain. is already in Hermite normal form, although neither pivot divides the other. The chain belongs to Smith normal form.

Rectangular and lower-rank versions use pivot positions and possible zero columns; see Characterization of integer Lattices. Transposed row conventions reverse the role of row and column operations. Smith normal form

Let

  • an integer matrix, with and rank over
  • the sublattice generated by its columns
  • and, for , the positive gcd of all minors of , called its determinantal divisors

Then

  1. there are unimodular matrices and such that
    with every other entry of zero. This is the Smith normal form.
  2. , so ; in particular the diagonal is unique, is the gcd of all entries when , and when .
  3. the quotient is
    The entries are its invariant factors; an entry contributes a zero summand.
Idea

Use both row and column versions of Euclid. Before freezing a pivot, require it to divide every entry of the remaining block. If it fails that test, bring an offending entry into its row and run Euclid again. That extra test produces the divisibility chain.

Note
  • Allowed moves. Swap rows or columns, change their signs, or add an integer multiple of one to another. As in Hermite normal form, never divide a row or column by a nonunit.
  • Meaning of the two sides. has the same column span as , whereas generates . The map is an isomorphism of quotients. If one keeps the abstract ambient module fixed, describes a change of ambient coordinates. Equivalently, .
  • Zero rank. For , the list of nonzero pivots is empty, , and the quotient is .
  • Other coefficient rings. Smith normal form exists over any PID, with diagonal entries unique up to units. The explicit decreasing-remainder algorithm below uses the Euclidean division of ; it also adapts to Euclidean domains, while a general PID need not supply such a division algorithm.

    1. Choose a pivot. If the remaining block is zero, stop. Otherwise move any nonzero entry to by row and column swaps and make it positive, calling it .
    2. Clear column by Euclid. For each , write the current , with , and apply . If , swap and restart with the smaller pivot .
    3. Clear row by Euclid. Once column is zero below the pivot, apply the corresponding divisions for . A nonzero remainder is swapped into and the column-clearing step restarts: a column swap may reintroduce entries below the pivot. A zero remainder clears an entry without disturbing the zeros in column .
    4. Test divisibility of the whole remaining block (crux). Once the pivot row and column are cleared, the active block is . If divides every entry of , accept and recurse on . Otherwise choose in not divisible by and apply . The pivot stays , while the entry in position becomes . Write with , perform , and swap . The new positive pivot is ; restart clearing.
    5. Termination and the chain. Every restart strictly decreases a positive integer pivot. Between restarts there are only finitely many entries to clear or test, so each stage terminates. When is accepted, every entry of the next block is a multiple of . Subsequent integer row and column operations preserve that property, so its next nonzero pivot is a multiple of . Earlier isolated pivots remain untouched. Rank preservation gives exactly nonzero pivots, and the product of all operations gives .
  • Each allowed row or column operation expresses every new -minor as an integer linear combination of old -minors, by multilinearity of the determinant. Applying its integral inverse gives the reverse containment, so their gcd is unchanged. For , the nonzero -minors are products with . The divisibility chain implies divides every such product, and it occurs as the first principal minor. Thus , proving the assertions and uniqueness.

Warning

A diagonal matrix need not be in Smith form. Stopping after clearing rows and columns misses the divisibility test. The Smith entries are also generally different from the Hermite pivots; a common determinant does not determine either list.

Ideal criterion via multiplication matrices

Let

  • a commutative ring with identity, free of finite rank over , with fixed ordered basis , for example an order
  • a full-rank sublattice, with ordered basis , where has nonzero determinant and its columns are the ambient coordinates of the
  • the matrix of multiplication by in , so its -th column contains the coordinates of

Then the following are equivalent:

  1. is an ideal of
  2. for every
  3. divides every entry of for every , where is the adjugate matrix, satisfying .
Idea

A lattice is already closed under addition. It is an ideal precisely when multiplication by every ring element preserves it. The conjugated matrices express multiplication in the lattice basis, so their entries must be integers.

Proof

  • an element with lattice coordinates has ambient coordinates . Multiplication by gives ambient coordinates , hence lattice coordinates . Thus iff , equivalently every column of is integral. Since every is an integer combination of the , these finitely many conditions are equivalent to .
  • substitute . The numerator is an integer matrix, so the quotient is integral exactly when every numerator entry is divisible by .
A finite ideal test in any rank
  1. Express the products in the fixed ambient basis to obtain the multiplication matrices .
  2. Obtain a basis matrix for the candidate lattice using column Hermite reduction if needed.
  3. For each , solve exactly over and test every entry of for integrality; equivalently, use the integer divisibility test in . Accept precisely when all tests pass.

This tests the extra multiplication conditions that distinguish an ideal from an arbitrary sublattice. Hermite triangularity alone does not imply them.

Note
  • Fewer multiplication matrices. It suffices to test any set of ring generators over : stability under their multiplication maps implies stability under sums and compositions, hence under multiplication by every polynomial in the generators. For , one matrix suffices.
  • No maximality hypothesis. The criterion applies to nonmaximal orders too; it uses only the free additive structure and multiplication, with no Dedekind hypothesis.
  • Basis conventions. need not be triangular. Replacing it by for a unimodular replaces by , preserving integrality. Smith normal form instead describes the additive quotient ; its divisibility chain is a different condition.

The inverse of an ideal, explicitly

Point hands the inverse of any non-zero ideal in closed form,
which is Invertibility of ideals in Dedekind domains made concrete for a quadratic field: inverting is conjugating, up to a rational factor that dies in the class group. That is why point of The form class group as a Picard group reads "the inverse class is the class of the conjugate ideal", and why on forms the inverse of is : conjugating the ideal reverses the orientation of its basis, which negates the middle coefficient.

Only the maximal order behaves like this

For a non maximal order , i.e. for not fundamental, the identity fails in general: by point of Realizing a quadratic form as a norm form, for a form of discriminant ,
and an imprimitive form gives an ideal that is a module over a strictly larger order, hence not invertible. The proof above breaks exactly at the cancellation step, which used the Dedekind property. So this note is the reason the theorem of the next chapter needs fundamental, while The form class group as a Picard group has to restrict to invertible ideals instead.

From ideal multiplication to composition

The principal-ideal formula relates the ideal norm to the absolute value of the field norm. In degree two, field-norm multiplicativity and this theorem give Ideal multiplication gives a direct composition of normalized norm forms: divide by and compute the two slice determinants in positively oriented bases. This proves the compatibility used in The narrow class group is isomorphic to the form class group and Gauss composition.

Note
  • Fractional ideals. The same product formula holds with integer prime exponents for fractional ideal norms, by clearing denominators.
  • Dependency order. The arbitrary-degree proof uses no conjugate-product formula. It is the input to Product of all Galois conjugates of an ideal, whose proof must not be used in reverse to establish this theorem.
Warning

This theorem concerns ideals of the full ring of integers. For a nonmaximal order, multiplicativity holds when one factor is invertible but can fail for arbitrary ideals; see the nonmaximal-order discussion.
